name: Bodleian Library
label: Bodleian Library
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'University Church of St Mary the Virgin' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'St Mary and St John Church of England Primary School' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/62123: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bodleian Library' (83 m across).
notes: Historic library with a famous quadrangle.

text.description: The Bodleian Library is the University of Oxford's main research library, founded in 1602 by Sir Thomas Bodley and one of the oldest libraries in Europe. It is not a single building but a group of five near Broad Street. The round, domed Radcliffe Camera is the one most visitors photograph. It dates from the 18th century and stands in Radcliffe Square, with the 17th-century Schools Quadrangle close behind it. Duke Humfrey's Library, the 15th-century reading room completed in 1488, is part of the same group. The Camera photographs well because the old college buildings around the square frame the dome. From the steps you can see the Camera between Brasenose College on the right and the Old Schools Quadrangle behind it, with the dome as the main subject. For a different view, walk to Brasenose Lane, where the Camera slowly appears at the end of a narrow lane. It is also popular, so expect other people in your shot. The church tower gives a view down over the Camera and the surrounding roofs. Visiting the tower may involve a fee, so check the official site before you go. These are all views of the outside only. The inside of the Camera is restricted to readers and the extended tour.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Oxford, around Radcliffe Square, close to Broad Street. The University Church of St Mary the Virgin stands on the High Street side of the square.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the High Street in central Oxford and find the University Church of St Mary the Virgin. The church steps on the south side of Radcliffe Square are the place to stand, and the Radcliffe Camera is in the square next to it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the dome, Brasenose College and the Old Schools Quadrangle all fit in the frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the dome and its stonework. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole square, and keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on University Church of St Mary the Virgin (south side of Radcliffe Square, church steps). The Radcliffe Camera framed between Brasenose College on the right and the Old Schools Quadrangle behind it, with the dome as the main subject. On the steps of the University Church of St Mary the Virgin, on the south side of Radcliffe Square. From the steps the Radcliffe Camera sits between Brasenose College on the right and the Old Schools Quadrangle behind, with the dome as the main subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the dome slightly off-centre, with Brasenose College forming the right-hand edge. Hold the phone level to keep the vertical lines straight. For a second shot, try Brasenose Lane, where the Camera comes into view at the end of the narrow lane and the walls on each side lead the eye towards it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright so the stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as people often walk through the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is usually quieter, which helps in the square and especially in Brasenose Lane. Soft daylight suits the stonework well.

text.access_note: Radcliffe Square can be seen from outside, but the Radcliffe Camera's interior is restricted to readers and the extended tour, and the church tower is a paid climb, so check the official site before you go.

name: Christ Church, Oxford
label: Christ Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'St Aldate's' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of St Aldate's nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/15595647: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Christ Church' (479 m across).
notes: Grand college seen in the Harry Potter films.

text.description:
Christ Church is one of the best-known colleges of the University of Oxford, and its main gate is the classic place to start. Above the entrance arch rises Tom Tower, designed by Sir Christopher Wren, and behind the gate lies Tom Quad, the largest quadrangle in Oxford. Henry VIII founded the college in 1546. It is unusual because its chapel is also Oxford's cathedral. The buildings have appeared in films such as Harry Potter, which helps explain why it is the most popular Oxford college for tourists.

From the pavement on St Aldate's, directly opposite the Tom Gate entrance, you get a straight-on, symmetrical view. The full height of the tower sits above the arch, with the wings either side. It is a simple, balanced picture that works well on a phone, and you only need to photograph from outside. If you want a change, Pembroke Square gives a view of the entrance and tower framed by neighbouring buildings. Christ Church Meadow shows the towers and the cathedral spire rising behind open grass, sometimes with cattle in the foreground.

A small piece of trivia: the bell in the tower, Great Tom, rings 101 times each evening at 9:05 pm. St Aldate's is a busy road with buses, so cross with care, and stay on the pavement and watch for buses while framing.
text.geographic_location: Christ Church is in central Oxford, on the east side of St Aldate's, with Christ Church Meadow stretching out behind it. The Tom Gate entrance faces the street.
text.directions_text: Head for St Aldate's in the centre of Oxford and look for the tall Tom Tower above the college gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full gate and tower. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if passers-by or parked vehicles stop you stepping back far enough. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the upper stages of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on St Aldate's (directly opposite the Tom Gate entrance, on the pavement across the road). A head-on, symmetrical view of the full height of Tom Tower above the college's main gate, with the entrance arch and flanking wings below it. On St Aldate's, on the pavement directly opposite the Tom Gate entrance, looking east across the road to the gate and the tower above it. Stay on the pavement and cross carefully, as buses use this road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the arch on the centre line so the two wings balance left and right. Hold the phone level, because tilting it upwards makes the tower lean inwards. Keep the whole tower in the shot, with a little sky above the top. For a different view, try Pembroke Square or Christ Church Meadow.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the tower keeps its colour. Take a few frames, as people often walk through the gateway.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day for fewer people on the pavement. If you stay until the evening, use night mode with the phone braced against a wall or post.

text.access_note: You can photograph the gate and tower from the public pavement on St Aldate's without a ticket, but going inside the college needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day is usually quieter on the pavement opposite the gate.
Tilting the phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean inwards.
St Aldate's is in the centre of Oxford and Tom Gate faces onto it, on the east side of the street.

name: Ashmolean Museum
label: Ashmolean Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1337584: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ashmolean Museum' (130 m across).
notes: The oldest university museum in the world.

text.description: The Ashmolean Museum stands on Beaumont Street, in the heart of Oxford. Its grand classical front, with tall columns and a wide set of steps, makes it one of the easiest buildings in the city to photograph. The building you see today dates from 1841 to 1845 and was designed by Charles Cockerell. It is Britain's first public museum, a title that goes back to its first home on Broad Street, which opened in 1683 to house the collection Elias Ashmole gave to the University of Oxford. Part of the same building, on the corner with St Giles', is the Taylor Institution, which uses the same Ionic style, so the long frontage has a pleasing rhythm of columns that suits a wide photo. The stone is a calm, even colour and the symmetry is strong, so a straight-on shot looks tidy and balanced with very little effort. The building is large, so the key is to decide whether you want the whole frontage or just a detail, such as the columns, the steps or the entrance. Stand back far enough to keep the vertical lines straight, and watch for people on the steps, who add a sense of scale. Inside, the museum holds art and archaeology, but this spot is about the outside view. Check the official site before you go if you plan to step inside, as access and any photography rules can change.
text.geographic_location: On Beaumont Street in central Oxford, at the corner with St Giles', with the Taylor Institution forming one wing of the same building.
text.directions_text: No railway station or tram stop is listed close to this spot, so start from central Oxford and head for Beaumont Street, which is easy to find on any map. The phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so once you are on Beaumont Street you are in the right place. If you are coming from further out, use a map app on your phone and navigate to Beaumont Street. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full frontage, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the columns and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Move back across the street a little if you want the whole front in one shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the roofline up with a horizontal line so the building does not lean. Keep the phone level and at chest height to limit the converging of the vertical lines. Try one wide shot with the steps in the foreground, then a closer one of the column rows with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the front of the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright and washes out the stone. Use ultra-wide only when you really need it, as it can bend the edges of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light on an overcast day or in the morning or late afternoon usually flatters the stone; a quieter time of day makes it easier to get a clear view of the steps.

text.access_note: The building is a museum site, and access and photography rules can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Radcliffe Camera
label: Radcliffe Camera
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Radcliffe Square' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Radcliffe Square' (relation/54084): middle (129 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4884600: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Radcliffe Camera' (47 m across).
notes: Iconic domed library on Radcliffe Square.

text.description: The Radcliffe Camera is a round Baroque library building in the middle of Oxford. James Gibbs designed it, and it was built between 1737 and 1749. It was paid for from the estate of the physician John Radcliffe, who left £40,000 when he died in 1714. Today it is a reading room for the Bodleian Library and is not open to the public, so this is a spot for exterior photos only. It photographs well because it stands apart from the buildings around it. The round Portland stone drum and the dome make a simple, strong shape, and the tower of St Mary the Virgin and the neighbouring colleges sit around it as a frame. Radcliffe Square is the classic place to take the picture, and you can see the building freely from there at any time. The cobbles and the surrounding walls add texture to the foreground. Brasenose College lies to the west and All Souls College to the east, so you can use their stonework to give the shot some depth. If you want a different angle, try Catte Street, where college walls and rooflines frame the dome. Brasenose Lane gives a reveal shot, with the dome slowly coming into view at the end of the narrow lane. Photography is not allowed inside the Camera. It is busiest from mid-morning, so go early if you want the square to yourself.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Oxford, in Radcliffe Square. It sits south of the Old Bodleian, north of the Church of St Mary the Virgin, and between Brasenose College and All Souls College.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is close enough to give as a starting point, so head for the centre of Oxford and walk into Radcliffe Square. The Camera stands about 26 m to the east of it, only a few steps away. If you arrive by Catte Street or Brasenose Lane, you will see the dome appear ahead as you approach. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole dome and drum in from close up. Switch to the default lens (1x) when you step back, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome's details and the tower behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Radcliffe Square (open cobbled square, facing the dome). The full round dome and Portland stone drum of the Camera, with St Mary the Virgin's tower and the surrounding colleges around it. On the open cobbled square facing the dome. You will see the full round dome and stone drum, with the tower of St Mary the Virgin and the surrounding colleges around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the drum up with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Keep the dome central and use the cobbles as a foreground. For a different shot, try Catte Street for the dome framed by college walls, or Brasenose Lane for the dome appearing at the end of the narrow lane.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dome to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out the pale stone. Avoid portrait mode here; it suits people better than buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the tour groups and crowds arrive. The square gets heavy with visitors from mid-morning.

text.access_note: The square is public and free to walk into, but the Camera's interior is not open to the public and cannot be photographed, so check the official Bodleian site before you go if you are interested in a tour.
claims_not_in_sources: From close up in the square, the full dome and drum may not fit in the default lens (1x) frame, so the ultra-wide (0.5x) helps.
Gridlines help keep the vertical lines of the building straight.
Lowering the exposure slider can stop a bright sky washing out pale stone.

name: Oxford Union
label: Oxford Union
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'St Michael's Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of St Michael's Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11644599: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Oxford Union' (97 m across).
notes: Famous debating society.

text.description:
The Oxford Union is a debating society founded in 1823, and its buildings are tucked into the middle of the city. The main block is Venetian Gothic, and a 1910 extension rises above the street beside it. The society commissioned Benjamin Woodward to design its first buildings, which opened in 1857. Alfred Waterhouse's debating chamber followed in 1878 and was then the largest purpose-built debating chamber in the world. The original chamber became the library, which now holds over 60,000 volumes.

It photographs well because the street frames it. The Gothic brick and stonework sit above the pavement with the Oxford street line leading your eye along. Treat it as a good street-level photo rather than a grand set-piece view. The Union is a private members' society, so its gardens, courtyards and interiors are not open to casual photographers. Take your pictures from the public street and keep clear of doorways.

If you have a few spare minutes, Frewin Court is a short alternative. It gives a narrow view down the lane towards the debating hall on one side of the passage.
text.geographic_location: In central Oxford, beside Frewin Court. The main block faces St Michael's Street, with the debating chamber set back off the street.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for St Michael's Street in central Oxford and find the Union's main block. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the front of the building with the street around it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the full height in. Use telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for details in the brick and stonework above the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on St Michael's Street (north pavement, facing the south side where the Union's main block stands). The Union's Venetian Gothic main block and its 1910 extension rising above the street, framed by the Oxford street line. From there the Union's Venetian Gothic main block and its 1910 extension rise above the street in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them, holding the phone level so the walls do not lean. Let the line of the street lead into the frame. If you want a different angle, Frewin Court gives a narrow view along the lane towards the debating hall, which sits on one side of the passage.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. Wait for a gap in passers-by before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight suits it best, because you can see the detail in the brick and stone. Early in the day is likely to be quieter on the street.

text.access_note: The Union is a private members' society, so photograph from the public street only; check the official site before you go if you hope to see inside.

name: Pitt Rivers Museum
label: Pitt Rivers Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/99873920: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pitt Rivers Museum' (74 m across).
notes: Crowded Victorian museum of world cultures.

text.description: The Pitt Rivers Museum holds the University of Oxford's archaeological and anthropological collections, and it photographs well because of how it is laid out. The main exhibition space is a large, rectangular, colonnaded room with two mezzanine levels, a tall vaulted ceiling and row upon row of glass display cases. The museum arranges objects by how they were used rather than by age or origin, so you often see many versions of one kind of tool or artefact side by side. That repetition gives you tidy, pattern-filled close-ups. The largest object on display is a Haida house post (a totem pole), 11.36 m high. It was bought by Edward Burnett Tylor and brought to the museum in 1901, and it makes a natural centrepiece for a tall, upright photo. The museum was founded in 1884 by Augustus Pitt Rivers, and the building was finished in 1886. It began with about 22,000 items and now holds more than 600,000. The museum sits behind the Oxford University Museum of Natural History and is entered through that building. Inside, expect crowded cases, glass reflections and fairly dim corners. Step back to take in the whole room, then move in on single cases and labels. Displays are changed from time to time, so what you see may differ from older photos. Check the official site before you go for entry details and any photography rules.
text.geographic_location: In Oxford, immediately east of the Oxford University Museum of Natural History, which is the only way in.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed for this spot. Make your way to the Oxford University Museum of Natural History, through which the Pitt Rivers Museum is entered. Follow the signs inside. The phone icon on the map is within the museum itself, so there is no extra walk once you are in. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tall room, the mezzanine levels and the totem pole in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for single display cases. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for small objects and labels without leaning on the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Pick a spot in the main colonnaded room where you can see the floor, the cases and the upper levels. Then turn to face the totem pole.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright for the totem pole and tilt up slowly so the top is not cut off. Turn on gridlines to keep the pillars and case edges straight. For case photos, stand square-on and get close to the glass. Angle the phone slightly to avoid your own reflection, or keep the lens near the glass if that is allowed. Pick one type of object and photograph the repeated rows for a pattern shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright object to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so lit cases do not wash out. In dim corners use night mode, and hold the phone against a rail or your body to keep it steady. Panorama is rarely useful indoors, so skip it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the room is quieter so you can stand back and get clear views. Opening times vary, so check the official site before you go.

text.access_note: This museum is entered through the Oxford University Museum of Natural History, so check the official site before you go for entry details and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Lighting inside the main gallery is fairly dim in places.
Glass display cases can cause reflections in phone photos.
The museum is likely to be quieter at off-peak times.

name: Martyrs' Memorial, Oxford
label: Martyrs' Memorial
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'St Giles'' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of St Giles' and Beaumont Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/16252895: the OpenStreetMap point 'Martyrs' Memorial'.
notes: Gothic Revival monument on St Giles'.

text.description:
The Martyrs' Memorial is a tall stone Gothic monument that stands in the middle of a busy Oxford junction, where St Giles', Magdalen Street and Beaumont Street meet, just west of Balliol College. It remembers Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley, the three Protestant churchmen executed in the 1550s. George Gilbert Scott designed it, and it was finished in 1843. He modelled it on the medieval Eleanor crosses, which is why it looks a little like a cathedral spire set down in the street. Henry Weekes carved the three statues, and the monument is listed at Grade II*. The Oxford Preservation Trust restored it, and the finished work was unveiled in January 2003.

It photographs well because the pointed spire and carved detail stand out against the plainer buildings around it, and the Ashmolean sits across the road on Beaumont Street. From the junction you can fit the monument, the statues and the street scene into one frame. The actual execution site is close by in Broad Street and is marked by an iron cross sunk into the road, so it is worth a look if you are walking on.

The junction is busy with buses and scooters, so frame your shots carefully and keep an eye on the traffic. Trees in the graveyard on the memorial's own side can block the view, so the junction gives the clearest picture.
text.geographic_location: In central Oxford, at the southern end of St Giles', where Magdalen Street and Beaumont Street meet, just west of Balliol College and opposite the Ashmolean.
text.directions_text: No railway station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Oxford and walk to the junction of St Giles', Magdalen Street and Beaumont Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole monument and the street around it in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues and carved detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of St Giles' and Beaumont Street (the junction at the south end of St Giles', where Magdalen Street also meets). The memorial standing at the crossroads with the Ashmolean and the street scene around its base. Stand on St Giles', at the junction at the south end where Magdalen Street also meets. The memorial rises a little to the south-east of you, with the Ashmolean and the street scene around its base. From here you see the monument's full Gothic height with the Cranmer statue facing you, and the street opening up towards it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the spire up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Keep the base and some of the street in the frame, as the junction gives the monument its setting. For a second view, try Magdalen Street, where the memorial is seen from that side with the Balliol College buildings behind you. Wait for gaps in the traffic and stay on the pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone on your screen to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Use the telephoto for the statues rather than walking into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is likely to be quieter, with fewer people and less traffic in the shot.

text.access_note: The memorial stands in the open at a public street junction, so you can photograph it from the street; check the official site before you go if you plan to visit anything nearby that may be ticketed.

name: Sheldonian Theatre
label: Sheldonian Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Broad Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Broad Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27582068: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sheldonian Theatre' (42 m across).
notes: Wren-designed ceremonial hall ringed by stone heads.

text.description:
The Sheldonian Theatre is a handsome 17th-century building in the heart of Oxford, designed by Christopher Wren for the University and built between 1664 and 1669. It is named after Gilbert Sheldon, who paid for almost all of it. It was built for degree ceremonies, and it is still used for ceremonies, concerts and lectures. It seats up to 700 people. The D-shaped plan and the eight-sided cupola on the roof make it easy to recognise, and it is a Grade I listed building.

It photographs well from the street because the facade sits among other fine buildings. The Clarendon Building is to the left at the front and the Old Ashmolean Building is to the right. From Broad Street you can fit the theatre and the Clarendon Building beyond it into one frame, with the street leading the eye towards them. This is the classic street-level view of the theatre.

Stand on the pavement and keep your phone level so the stonework stays upright. Pedestrians and cyclists pass all day, so wait for a gap or let a few people walk through as part of the scene. If you want a different angle, try Catte Street or the covered bridge known as the Bridge of Sighs (check the name on a map), covered in the phone section below. The cupola has views over central Oxford, but check the official site before you go for access and visiting arrangements.
text.geographic_location: On Broad Street, in the centre of Oxford, beside the Clarendon Building and the Old Ashmolean Building, adjacent to the Bodleian grounds.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop listed near here; head for the centre of Oxford and walk to Broad Street, outside Trinity College. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street view. If the pavement is busy or you cannot step back far enough, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the facade and the Clarendon Building in. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the carved details and the cupola.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Broad Street (looking east from outside Trinity College, with the theatre on the right). The Sheldonian's facade on Broad Street, with the Clarendon Building beyond, in the classic street-level view. Looking east from outside Trinity College, with the theatre on your right. You will see the Sheldonian's facade with the Clarendon Building beyond it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building edges up with the vertical lines so the walls do not lean. Keep the street running into the frame as a lead-in. For a less crowded angle, try Catte Street, looking at the facade from across the road. You can also try the covered bridge known as the Bridge of Sighs (check the name on a map), which frames the theatre from beneath.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail. If your phone has a Live Photo or motion option, it can help you pick a frame without passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even daylight suits the pale stone.

text.access_note: The facade is visible from the public street, but the theatre closes at times for ceremonies and concerts and visitor access to the building and cupola may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Oxford University Museum of Natural History
label: Natural History Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25999883: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Oxford University Museum of Natural History' (109 m across).
notes: Neo-Gothic museum hall with an iron and glass roof.

text.description: The Oxford University Museum of Natural History is a neo-Gothic building on Parks Road, designed mostly by Benjamin Woodward with Thomas Newenham Deane and opened in 1860. The idea was to bring the university's scattered science teaching and collections together around one central display area. The best pictures are inside the great square court. It has a glass roof held up by slim cast iron pillars, with arcades running around the ground and first floors. The stone columns are each cut from a different British stone, and the ironwork and carving are decorated with leaves and branches. Statues of famous scientists stand around the ground floor. It also hosted the well-known 1860 evolution debate, and the museum and the neighbouring Pitt Rivers Museum are both Grade I listed. Much of the ornamentation was never completed because funding ran out. For a phone, this is a place of repeating arches, glass and pillars, so look for strong lines and symmetry. Use the ultra-wide lens for the whole court, then move in for single carvings, column tops and statues. The displays are being renewed in phases, with the project due to finish in July 2026, so some cases may look different from older photos. Check what is allowed for photography before you start shooting indoors.
text.geographic_location: On Parks Road in central Oxford, in the university's science district, with the Pitt Rivers Museum built onto its east side.
text.directions_text: No railway station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head to Parks Road in central Oxford, where the museum stands. Once there, the phone icon on the map is at the middle of the museum building. Look for the large neo-Gothic building on Parks Road. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the glass-roofed court and the long arcades. Switch to the default lens (1x) for statues and arches, and to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved leaves, column tops and details high on the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Shoot the court from where you can see the full width of the glass roof, and keep the pillars in a line on each side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the pillars and arcades with the vertical lines so the building does not look tilted. Include one statue or one carved column in the foreground for a sense of scale. For detail shots, choose a single stone column or carving and fill the frame with it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of the roof or windows, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the glass does not turn white. Tap on a statue or column if you want it sharp. Hold the phone steady against a pillar or rail for darker corners, and try night mode if the light is low.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit in daylight, when the glass roof lets in the most light. A quieter moment makes it easier to photograph the court without people in the way.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so access, photography rules and any ticketing may vary: check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The glass roof lets in plenty of daylight, so daytime is the best time for interior photographs.
The court is likely to be quieter at some times of day than others, which helps with photographs without people.
Photography rules inside the museum may vary, so visitors should check them.

name: Oxford Botanic Garden
label: Botanic Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Magdalen Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Magdalen Bridge' (way/1154991954): middle (153 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/16470745: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'University of Oxford Botanic Garden' (261 m across).
notes: The oldest botanic garden in Britain.

text.description: Oxford Botanic Garden is the oldest botanic garden in Great Britain, founded in 1621 as a physic garden for growing medicinal plants. It sits on the bank of the River Cherwell, at the north-east corner of Christ Church Meadow, and packs more than 5,000 plant species into about 1.8 hectares. For a phone photo, the best view from outside the walls is the classic postcard angle from Magdalen Bridge. From there you can see the garden's riverside edge, punts drifting on the Cherwell, and Magdalen College's tower rising behind the trees. It puts water, greenery and a famous Oxford landmark in one frame without any fuss. If you go inside, the Danby Gate at the front entrance is worth a close shot. Nicholas Stone designed it in 1632-33, and it is a Grade I listed structure with statues and a bust set into the stonework. Inside, a stone archway in the garden wall can frame the plants like a secret garden. A quieter alternative is Christ Church Meadow, where you can look across open grass to the garden's green edge and trees. Keep your phone ready for passing punts, and take a few frames rather than one, as the boats keep moving.
text.geographic_location: The garden is in Oxford, on the bank of the River Cherwell next to Christ Church Meadow. Magdalen College and Magdalen Bridge are close by.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops listed for this spot, so head for Magdalen Bridge. From there it is about 2 minutes on foot to the garden. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the garden edge, the river and the tower in one frame. If you want the tower to look closer, try the telephoto (2x-3x). Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you need to fit in more of the river, and keep straight lines away from the edges so they don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Magdalen Bridge (south end, looking back across the Cherwell toward the garden). The Botanic Garden's riverside edge with punts on the Cherwell, with Magdalen College's tower rising behind the garden. At the south end, and look back across the Cherwell. The garden's riverside edge is to the west, with punts on the water and Magdalen College's tower rising behind the garden.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the river in the lower third, with the garden's trees and the tower above it. Wait for a punt to drift into the lower part of the frame to give a sense of scale. For a different shot, try the stone archway inside the garden wall as a frame for the plants, or Christ Church Meadow for a quiet view across the grass of the garden's green edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower or the trees to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. Try a Live Photo to catch the punts moving, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time is given for this view. Try early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the bridge may be quieter.

text.access_note: The bridge and the meadow are public land, but entry to the garden itself (walled garden and glasshouses) is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer, and the bridge may be quieter then.
Punts pass along the Cherwell regularly, so a boat may drift into the frame.

name: Covered Market, Oxford
label: Covered Market
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/3663178: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Covered Market' (134 m across).
notes: Historic indoor market with food stalls.

text.description:
The Covered Market is a roofed market in the middle of Oxford, packed with small shops and stalls under one large structure. It has been trading since it officially opened on 1 November 1774, and it was set up to move untidy stalls off the main streets. John Gwynn, who also designed Magdalen Bridge, drew up the plans and designed the High Street front with its four entrances. The building has been Grade II listed since 2000. Today around half of the traders sell food, with greengrocers, butchers (some making the Oxford sausage), bakeries and sandwich shops, plus newer gift shops.

It photographs well because of its variety. Shop fronts, hanging signs, piled-up produce and the long covered lanes give you plenty of colour and a strong sense of place. The outline is about 134 m across, so there is room to wander and look for different angles. A good approach is to start with one wide shot that shows the lane stretching away, then move in on details such as a cheese counter, a flower stall or a hand-painted sign.

Keep your phone steady, tap on the brightest part of your subject so the shop lights don't blow out, and be considerate around the stalls. Ask before taking close photos of traders or customers, and don't block the walkways. Opening arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In central Oxford, just north of the High Street towards its western end, between Cornmarket Street and Turl Street. Market Street runs along the north side.
text.directions_text: Head for the High Street in central Oxford, towards its western end, or for Market Street on the north side. Both have entrances into the market, and there is another from Cornmarket Street through the Golden Cross alley. If you are coming by taxi or hired scooter, ask for the High Street or Market Street and walk in through any of the entrances to reach the phone icon on the map in the middle of the market. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long covered lanes, then use the default lens (1x) for shop fronts and stalls. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details like signs and produce without leaning over the counters.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Turn on the spot to find the lane with the best depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line a lane up with the centre so it leads the eye into the shot. Include a hanging sign or a stall edge in the foreground for depth. For a detail shot, fill the frame with one counter and let the background blur a little.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the lights don't wash out. If it feels dim, let night mode work and rest your elbows against your body to keep still. Portrait mode suits a single item on a counter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer, so the lanes are easier to photograph without crowds. Daylight from the entrances helps, but the light inside is mostly artificial at any time.

text.access_note: A public market with several street entrances, but opening arrangements can vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The lanes inside are usually busier around lunchtime and at weekends, and calmer earlier in the day.
The light inside is mostly artificial, with some daylight near the entrances.
Traders and customers may prefer to be asked before being photographed up close.

name: Bridge of Sighs, Oxford
label: Bridge of Sighs
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'New College Lane' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Catte Street and New College Lane (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W62333303 (The Bridge of Sighs): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Covered bridge linking two parts of Hertford College.

text.description: The Bridge of Sighs is a bridge over New College Lane in central Oxford, and it is one of the easiest photos on the map to get right. The lane is so narrow that its high stone walls do much of the framing for you. They lead the eye straight to the bridge, and the upper windows of Hertford College show beyond it. Visitors cannot walk across the bridge because it is private Hertford College property. The outside of the bridge and the lane are public and free to photograph at any time, so this is a photo to take from the street rather than from the bridge itself. The classic angle is from the Catte Street end of New College Lane, looking east along it. Stand where the lane walls frame both sides, keep the bridge in the middle and let the buildings beyond sit behind it. If the lane is busy, wait a moment for a gap in the passing people, or include a few of them for a sense of scale. For a quieter, less common view, try Queen's Lane, where the Bodleian Library walls sit behind the bridge. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, because the lane is tight and small changes in position alter how much of the surrounding roofline you capture.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Oxford, where New College Lane runs east from Catte Street. The bridge is part of Hertford College and spans the lane.
text.directions_text: Head for Catte Street in central Oxford. Turn north off Catte Street into New College Lane. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the bridge framed by the lane walls. Try 2x if your phone has it, to bring the bridge closer and fill the frame without moving. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of wall and roofline, as it can stretch the edges of the lane.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Catte Street and New College Lane (Catte Street end of the lane, looking east along it). The bridge framed by the narrow lane walls, with upper Hertford College windows visible beyond it. Stand on New College Lane, at the Catte Street end, and look east along the lane.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the bridge up with the centre of the frame, keeping the lane walls roughly symmetrical on each side. Hold the phone level so the walls do not lean. For a different view, walk to Queen's Lane, where the bridge appears with the Bodleian Library walls behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky at the end of the lane looks washed out. Taking a few frames in a row helps you get one without passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is usually calmer, and gives you the best chance of an empty lane. The lane is narrow and often shaded, so check how the light looks on your screen before you shoot.

text.access_note: The lane is a public thoroughfare and free to photograph from, but the bridge itself is private Hertford College property and cannot be crossed by visitors.
claims_not_in_sources: The lane is often busy with passers-by during the day.
Early morning is usually quieter in the lane.
The narrow lane is often in shade, so the sky at the far end can look much brighter than the walls.
An ultra-wide lens can stretch the edges of a frame in a narrow lane.

name: Oxford Castle
label: Oxford Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quaking Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Quaking Bridge' (way/29034234): middle (9 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/29089712: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Oxford Castle Quarter' (213 m across).
notes: Norman castle mound with a restored prison.

text.description:
Oxford Castle is a large, partly ruined medieval castle on the western side of central Oxford. It was begun in the early 1070s by the Norman baron Robert D'Oyly the elder, who used a branch of the Thames, now called the Castle Mill Stream, to help form a moat. The tallest survivor is St George's Tower, built of coral rag stone. It is now thought to be a Saxon watch tower from around 1020 that the castle later absorbed. In later centuries the site became the county prison, which closed in 1996 and was redeveloped as a hotel and visitor attraction. The medieval remains are Grade I listed and a Scheduled Monument.

For a phone photo, the classic angle is from Quaking Bridge. The Castle Mill Stream fills the foreground and the stone tower rises behind it. The water gives you a natural leading line and a bit of reflection, and the tower is a simple, strong shape to build the picture around. Stand on the bridge, face the direction that brings the tower into frame and let the stream do the work. The interior is a separate matter, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside. If the bridge is busy, Pacey's Bridge is a quieter alternative for a calmer stretch of the same stream, looking towards the castle side of the water.
text.geographic_location: On the western side of central Oxford, in the Oxford Castle Quarter, which is about 213 m across. The Castle Mill Stream runs beside it, and the viewpoint is on a bridge over that stream.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so make your way on foot to the western side of central Oxford, around the Oxford Castle Quarter. From the bridge it is about 2 minutes on foot to the castle. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the stream, the tower and a little sky together. Switch to 2x if you want to fill the frame with the tower. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of water, because the tower will look small and distant.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Quaking Bridge (looking north or southeast across the Castle Mill Stream). The Castle Mill Stream in the foreground with St George's Tower of Oxford Castle rising behind it. Face whichever of those directions brings St George's Tower into frame, so the water is in the foreground and the tower rises behind it. For a quieter view of the stream, try Pacey's Bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower upright against a vertical line so it does not lean. Leave the lower third for the stream and let the tower sit off-centre. Wait for walkers to pass, or include one for scale. Pacey's Bridge offers a calmer alternative with a different stretch of water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky looks washed out. Try a Live Photo to catch ripples on the water, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the stonework, and early on weekdays the bridge is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The bridge and the view across the stream are in open public space, but the castle's interior, prison and tower climb are ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Magdalen Bridge
label: Magdalen Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Oxford Botanic Garden and Arboretum' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'University of Oxford Botanic Garden' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1154991954: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Magdalen Bridge' (153 m across).
notes: Starting point for punting on the Cherwell.

text.description: Magdalen Bridge carries the High Street over the River Cherwell on the eastern edge of central Oxford, right beside Magdalen College. It photographs well because several things line up in one frame: a long stone bridge, trees leaning over the water, and punts moored along the bank. The best view is from inside Oxford Botanic Garden and Arboretum, looking across the river, where the bridge sits with the water and Magdalen College behind it. The present bridge was built between 1772 and 1790 and has 11 arches of different sizes. It replaced a much older medieval stone bridge, and the first known mention of a bridge at this crossing dates from 1004. It was widened on the south side in 1882 to take a tramway, but the original design was kept. For photos, give yourself a little space and let the river fill the lower part of the frame, so the arches are reflected or at least sit above the water. The garden view works all year, but entry is charged and opening hours vary, so check the official site before you go. As an alternative, you can shoot from the bridge area itself, where overhanging trees and punts line the bank below. Keep well clear of the road, because the bridge carries traffic as well as pedestrians. It is also closed on the morning of 1 May for the May Morning crowds.
text.geographic_location: Magdalen Bridge is at the eastern end of the High Street, on the edge of Oxford city centre, next to Magdalen College. It crosses the River Cherwell, and the Oxford Botanic Garden and Arboretum is on the near side of the river.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the east end of Oxford's High Street. Follow the High Street towards Magdalen College to reach the bridge itself. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the bridge, river and punts in one frame. Try 2x if your phone has it, to pick out the arches and the college behind without the foreground crowding in. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move close to the water and want trees and punts in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Oxford Botanic Garden and Arboretum (view from inside the garden across the Cherwell). The bridge framed with the river, moored punts and Magdalen College behind it. From here the bridge lies to the east, framed with the river, moored punts and Magdalen College behind it. If you would rather not pay, the bridge area is the alternative, showing the overhanging trees and the colourful punts lined up along the bank below. A less usual angle on the bridge and punts may be possible from Angel & Greyhound Meadow, but the vegetation may block the view and the meadow often floods, so check conditions locally.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the line of arches along the upper third, with the water filling the lower two thirds. Let a punt or an overhanging branch sit in one corner to give depth. Wait for people to clear the bridge deck if you want a cleaner shot. For the alternative view, aim along the bank so the trees arch over the punts.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the sky and bright stonework keep their detail. If the water is still, a Live Photo can catch a gentle ripple or a punt drifting past, and you can choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning and late afternoon, when the sun lights up the bridge. The garden view can be shot at any time of year.

text.access_note: The best view is from inside the Oxford Botanic Garden and Arboretum, which charges entry and has varying opening hours, so check the official site before you go. The bridge itself is a public road, so stand clear of the traffic.

name: University Church of St Mary the Virgin
label: St Mary the Virgin
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/60903337: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Mary the Virgin' (67 m across).
notes: Its tower is a classic viewpoint over the city.

text.description: St Mary's is the University Church, and the spot where Oxford University began to take shape. It stands on the north side of the High Street, with Radcliffe Square just behind it. It photographs well because it offers two different pictures. On the High Street side there is the curly Baroque south porch, with twisting columns and a statue of the Virgin and Child in a shell-shaped niche. Above it, the tall spire rises from the 13th-century tower, with pinnacles, gargoyles and statues. The porch dates from 1637 and was designed by Nicholas Stone. The spire was added in the 1320s, and of its twelve statues only one is original; the rest were put up around 1894. The church has a long history. Meetings of the university were held here from at least 1252, and in 1555 it hosted the trial of the Oxford Martyrs. Both the porch and the spire reward a closer look. If you cannot fit the whole spire in from close range, step back or tilt the phone up slowly, keep the gridlines on, and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it does not lean. Then switch to the telephoto lens for the porch carvings and the statues high on the spire. The tower can be climbed for views over Radcliffe Square and the nearby colleges, but access may change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Oxford, on the north side of the High Street. Radcliffe Square is to the north, Catte Street to the east and St Mary's Passage to the west.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the High Street in central Oxford. The church is on the north side of the High Street, and you can also reach it on foot through St Mary's Passage from Radcliffe Square or along Catte Street. The phone icon on the map is at the church itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the porch and the base of the tower from close range. Use the default lens (1x) for a straighter, more natural view of the frontage. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the porch carvings, the statues and the top of the spire.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. To fit more in, step back a little along the High Street frontage for the porch and spire together, or walk round to Radcliffe Square for the spire and tower against the other buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the gridlines on and line the tower up with a vertical line so it does not appear to lean. Take one wide shot with the ultra-wide (0.5x), then a tighter one with the telephoto of the twisted columns and the statue niche. Keep your phone level and tilt it up only a little to avoid leaning verticals.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or a bright part of the stonework to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the pale stone keeps its detail against the sky. For the carved porch, tap on the statue niche to focus there.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the frame. Check how the light falls on the porch, as the frontage faces the High Street.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but the church and its tower are managed by the church, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.

name: Carfax Tower
label: Carfax Tower
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/469136813: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Carfax' (60 m across).
notes: Climb the tower for views over the city centre.

text.description:
Carfax Tower stands on the north-west corner of the crossroads that Oxford counts as the centre of the city. It is a square stone tower, and it is all that remains of St Martin's Church, a church that dates back to the 12th century and served for centuries as the city's own church. The tower is about 23 metres (74 feet) tall. The city council says no building in central Oxford should be taller, although one modern building has broken that rule. It is Grade II listed. It has a clock that chimes the quarter hours, and a ring of six bells that are rung on special occasions.

It photographs well because it stands alone at a busy meeting of four streets, so you can shoot it with the street scene around it: Cornmarket Street to the north, the High Street to the east, St Aldate's to the south and Queen Street to the west. The clock face is a good detail to pick out. You can also climb the tower for a view over the Oxford skyline, which is a second photo opportunity; check the official site before you go for current opening times.

For practical photo advice, stand back far enough to fit the whole tower in, and keep an eye on the traffic and the pavement crowds while you frame the shot. Behind the tower you can also see an old tombstone, which is a quiet detail if you want a closer picture.
text.geographic_location: Carfax Tower is in the very centre of Oxford, on the north-west corner of the Carfax crossroads where Cornmarket Street, the High Street, St Aldate's and Queen Street meet.
text.directions_text: Carfax is the crossroads at the centre of Oxford, so it is easy to reach on foot from anywhere in the city centre. Walk to the junction of Cornmarket Street, the High Street, St Aldate's and Queen Street and look for the tower on the north-west corner. If you are coming from further out, head for the city centre and walk the last part. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower and some of the street in close up, then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock face and the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the whole tower, step back across the junction until it fits in the frame. Take care with traffic and keep to the pavements.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines. Keep the phone upright rather than tilting it up, so the tower does not lean in the picture. Leave some street at the bottom of the frame so people can see where the tower sits. If you climb the tower, shoot the skyline with the default lens (1x) and keep your phone close to the opening.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright sky to set the focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone stays readable.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day usually means fewer people and less traffic around the crossroads. Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the stone than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The tower stands in an open public street, but climbing it is a separate visit, so check the official site before you go for current opening times.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day usually means fewer people and less traffic at the crossroads.
Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the stone than harsh midday sun.
The junction can be busy with traffic and pedestrians, so take care when stepping back to frame the tower.
From the crossroads you can step back across the junction to fit the whole tower into the frame.

name: Christ Church Meadow
label: Christ Church Meadow
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Broad Walk' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Broad Walk nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1102976: large area 'Christ Church Meadow' (1167 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Riverside meadow with walks and views of the spires.

text.description:
Christ Church Meadow is a broad, flat flood-meadow in the middle of Oxford, roughly triangular, with the River Thames (here called the Isis) and the River Cherwell along its edges and bounded by Christ Church college. It is a popular place for walking and picnics, and the lower parts are grazed by cattle, including Longhorn cows. That is what makes it work for photos: open grass and trees in the foreground, with college towers and the cathedral spire rising behind them.

The classic view is from Broad Walk, near the St Aldate's entrance, looking east across the meadow. Grass fills the foreground and the skyline sits behind the trees, so the picture has a clear front, middle and back. The meadow also has some history. James Sadler made the first balloon ascent by an Englishman from here on 4 October 1784, and a plaque records it. Rowing events such as Eights Week and Torpids are held on the Thames beside it.

For a phone, keep the horizon level using the gridlines and let the grass take up the lower third of the frame. If cattle are in view, they make a good foreground, but keep a respectful distance and use zoom rather than walking closer. Paths can be wet or closed when the meadow floods in winter. Drones are generally not permitted here.

If you want a different angle, try Christ Church Memorial Garden for the college over flower beds, or Merton Field for Merton College's chapel tower across open grass.
text.geographic_location: Christ Church Meadow lies in central Oxford, south of Christ Church college and the High Street, between the Thames (the Isis) and the Cherwell. Broad Walk runs along its northern edge, with Merton Field and Merton College beyond.
text.directions_text: Walk to the St Aldate's entrance beside Christ Church and go through the Christ Church War Memorial Garden onto Broad Walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the meadow and skyline. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and grass, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the towers and spire closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Broad Walk (near the St Aldate's entrance, looking east across the meadow). Grassy meadow in the foreground with the college towers and the cathedral spire rising behind the trees. Face east across the meadow, so the grass fills the foreground and the college towers and cathedral spire rise behind the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line, with grass filling the lower part of the frame. Let the trees frame the skyline and the spire sit just off-centre. If you want a different view, Christ Church Memorial Garden shows the college over the flower beds, and Merton Field shows Merton College's chapel tower across the open field.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the towers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. If cattle are in view, zoom in rather than walk closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. The gates are locked at night, so plan to be there in daylight.

text.access_note: The meadow is owned by Christ Church but open to the public during the day, with gates locked at night; paths may be wet or closed after flooding, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.
A telephoto lens will bring the towers and spire closer in the frame.

name: Magdalen College, Oxford
label: Magdalen College
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Magdalen Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Magdalen Bridge' (way/1154991954): middle (153 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/12605258: large area 'Magdalen College' (1184 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Famous tower, deer park and Addison's Walk.

text.description:
Magdalen College (say "MAWD-lin") is one of Oxford's best-known colleges, and its big, square tower is the part most visitors want to photograph. The college was founded in 1458 by William Waynflete, Bishop of Winchester, and it sits right beside the River Cherwell and next to the University of Oxford Botanic Garden. That setting is why the view works so well: the tower rises above the water, often with punts drifting below, and the glasshouses of the Botanic Garden sit to one side.

The tower also has a tradition behind it. Since the days of Henry VII, the college choir has sung from the top at 6 a.m. on May Morning. The tower is not open to the public, so your photos will be taken from outside. Inside the grounds there is a deer park and Addison's Walk, but access to the college itself may be limited, so check the official site before you go.

The classic spot is Magdalen Bridge, where you get the tower, river, punts and gardens in one frame. If the bridge is busy, two other angles work. From High Street you see the tower straight on, with the bridge end of the street in the frame. From Rose Lane, outside the Botanic Garden's walls, the tower rises behind the garden's trees and glasshouses, and it is usually less crowded than the bridge. Whichever you choose, take a few frames with and without people in them, and keep an eye on traffic when you stop to shoot.
text.geographic_location: On the River Cherwell, next to the University of Oxford Botanic Garden, by Magdalen Bridge.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed nearby, so walk to Magdalen Bridge from central Oxford. From there the main college buildings and the tower are about 194 m to the north-west, roughly 3 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the tower, river and punts in one frame. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer without walking into the road. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole bridge and river, because the tower will look small and the edges can stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Magdalen Bridge. The tower rising over the River Cherwell, with punts on the water and the Botanic Garden glasshouses to one side. From there the tower rises over the River Cherwell, with punts on the water and the Botanic Garden glasshouses to one side. Stay on the pavement and watch for traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower upright against a vertical line. Leave some river and punts at the bottom of the frame so the tower has something to rise from. For a quieter alternative, try Rose Lane, where the tower rises behind the Botanic Garden's trees and glasshouses, or High Street for a straight-on view of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Try a Live Photo when punts are passing, so you can pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer and gives softer light than midday. Avoid 1 May (May Morning), when the bridge is very crowded for the dawn gathering and good angles can be blocked.

text.access_note: Magdalen Bridge and High Street are public places. The Botanic Garden is paid entry and the tower is not open to the public. Access to the college grounds may be limited, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually calmer and has softer light than midday.
Access to the college grounds may be limited.
The ultra-wide lens makes distant subjects look smaller and can stretch the edges of the frame.

name: Broad Street, Oxford
label: Broad Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Clarendon Building' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Clarendon Building' (way/29387139): middle (52 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q60032: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Wide historic street lined with colleges and bookshops.

text.description: Broad Street is a wide, open street in the middle of Oxford, and that width is what makes it good for phone photos. You can step back far enough to get whole rows of old frontages in one frame. It was once called Horsemonger Street because it was Oxford's horse market, and it runs just north of the line of the old city wall. Today it is known for its bookshops, including the original Blackwell's at number 50. Residents traditionally call the street "The Broad". Three colleges sit along it: Balliol, Trinity and Exeter. At the eastern end stand some of the University's most important historic buildings. These include the Clarendon Building (built 1711–15 for the University press and designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor), the Sheldonian Theatre (built 1664–68 to a design by Christopher Wren) and the Old Ashmolean, built in 1683 and the world's first museum to open to the public. A cross of granite setts in the road opposite Balliol marks where the Oxford Martyrs were burnt in the 16th century. For the classic view, stand on the Clarendon Building steps, and let the street's historic facades frame the shot. Keep to the pavement and wait for gaps in the traffic and the passing groups. Trinity College also gives a long view down the street, with Exeter College on the right and the Sheldonian and Clarendon Building further off. If you would rather shoot the stonework close up, Balliol's frontage works well.
text.geographic_location: Broad Street is in central Oxford, just north of the former city wall. It runs between George Street to the west and Holywell Street to the east, with Balliol, Trinity and Exeter colleges along it and the Clarendon Building and Sheldonian Theatre at its eastern end.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right by this spot, so head for the centre of Oxford. Broad Street is just north of the old city wall, with the Clarendon Building at its eastern end. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full width of the street and the rows of facades. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as the Sheldonian's stone heads or the Clarendon Building's arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Clarendon Building (north-western corner of the steps, on the pavement rather than in the road). Broad Street running east with the Clarendon Building's arch and the Sheldonian Theatre beyond, framed by the street's historic facades. At the north-western corner, on the pavement rather than in the road. From here the street's historic facades frame the view, and the middle of Broad Street lies to the west. If the best spot is crowded with school or tour groups, try the opposite side of the road, and only from the pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the street up with the lower third of the frame, so the buildings rise on both sides. Keep the verticals straight by holding the phone level. For a different view, walk to Trinity College for a long eastward shot with Exeter College on the right and the Sheldonian and Clarendon Building beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then use the exposure slider to stop the sky washing out. Traffic and cyclists move through the frame, so take a few shots, or try a Live Photo and pick the cleanest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is likely to be quietest. Degree ceremonies at the Sheldonian bring crowds and gowns on many dates, which can add interest but makes it harder to get a clear view.

text.access_note: Broad Street is an open public street, but the colleges may close to visitors at short notice, so check before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From the Clarendon Building steps the view along Broad Street looks west, towards the subject.
Early morning is likely to be quieter than later in the day.
Holding the phone level helps keep building verticals straight.

name: New College, Oxford
label: New College
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Holywell Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Holywell Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/130536383: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'New College' (412 m across).
notes: Medieval cloisters and city wall garden.

text.description:
New College is one of Oxford's oldest colleges, despite the name. William of Wykeham, Bishop of Winchester, founded it in 1379, and it was the first Oxford college designed around a main quadrangle. Most of it sits behind high walls, so the best photo for most visitors is the street front on Holywell Street. This is the college's main public face in the city centre.

The frontage is a long Victorian range called 'New Buildings', built between 1872 and 1896. George Gilbert Scott designed part of it in 1872, and Basil Champneys designed the rest, including the Robinson Tower over the entrance gates (1885 and 1896). The tower above the gateway gives the picture a clear centre, and the stonework along the street gives it a strong sense of age and order.

Stand opposite the Robinson Tower entrance and keep the gateway in the middle of the frame, with the long street front running off to each side. It is a simple, tidy composition that works well on a phone. If you have time for a second angle, Bath Place, a side lane nearby, shows the college tower with the Turf Tavern in the foreground. Check the exact position on the map before you go.

The college grounds are not open public land, so the street is where most people will take their photos. Check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.
text.geographic_location: New College is in the centre of Oxford, between Holywell Street on its north side and New College Lane, which is known for Oxford's Bridge of Sighs. The Victorian entrance front faces Holywell Street.
text.directions_text: Head for Holywell Street in the centre of Oxford. The college front runs along the south side of Holywell Street, and the Robinson Tower gateway is the landmark to look for. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a calm, natural view of the tower and gateway. If you cannot fit the whole frontage in, try the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full street front and the tower together. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the tower and gateway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Holywell Street (opposite the Robinson Tower entrance, facing the college's Victorian frontage). The Robinson Tower gateway and the Victorian 'New Buildings' range of New College along the street front. Opposite the Robinson Tower entrance, and face south towards the college.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the gateway and tower in the centre and let the long stone front run to either side. Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the tower with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. For a different view, Bath Place nearby shows the New College tower from a side lane with the Turf Tavern in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its detail and the stone does not wash out. Avoid pinch-zooming past your phone's telephoto setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the street is quiet if you want fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: Holywell Street is a public street, but the college grounds are visitor-access areas rather than open public land, and photography is not generally allowed in the Great Hall or Chapel, so check the official site before you go.
